concepts.name: Constitutional Basis of the Union Budget
key_dimensions: Article 112: Annual Financial Statement — what it mandates vs. what 'Budget' colloquially includes
Distinction between Annual Financial Statement (constitutional document) and Budget (broader exercise including Finance Bill, Demands for Grants)
Role of Article 110 (Money Bill) vs. Article 109 (Finance Bill categories) in budget passage
UPSC trap: Budget is NOT a single document — it is a set of documents; Annual Financial Statement ≠ Appropriation Act

concepts.name: Revenue Budget vs. Capital Budget: Classification Logic
key_dimensions: Revenue receipts (tax + non-tax) and revenue expenditure — criteria for classification (recurrent nature, no asset creation)
Capital receipts (borrowings, disinvestment, recovery of loans) and capital expenditure — asset creation or liability reduction logic
UPSC trap: Grants-in-aid to states → Revenue expenditure for Centre even if used for capital purposes by states
Interest payments = Revenue expenditure; Loan repayment = Capital expenditure — common confusion point

concepts.name: Revenue Deficit: Definition, Implications, and FRBM Targets
key_dimensions: Revenue Deficit = Revenue Expenditure − Revenue Receipts; implies government borrowing to meet consumption needs
Effective Revenue Deficit (ERD): introduced in 2011-12 — excludes grants for capital asset creation from revenue deficit
Policy implication: persistent revenue deficit crowds out capital expenditure and signals fiscal stress
FRBM Act 2003 target trajectory for revenue deficit elimination; NK Singh Committee recommendations on ERD

concepts.name: Fiscal Deficit: Measurement, Financing, and Macroeconomic Implications
key_dimensions: Fiscal Deficit = Total Expenditure − Total Receipts (excluding borrowings); represents total borrowing requirement
Financing modes: market borrowings, small savings, RBI monetization — implications of each for inflation and crowding out
FRBM Act target: 3% of GDP; NK Singh Committee's escape clause (±0.5%) triggers and fiscal council proposal
UPSC trap: Fiscal deficit includes revenue deficit + capital expenditure financed by borrowing; NOT the same as debt

concepts.name: Primary Deficit: Concept and Significance
key_dimensions: Primary Deficit = Fiscal Deficit − Interest Payments; measures current fiscal burden excluding legacy debt servicing
Zero primary deficit implies government borrows only to pay interest — debt stabilization threshold concept
Distinction: High fiscal deficit with low primary deficit → inherited debt problem; High primary deficit → current profligacy
UPSC trap: Primary deficit can be zero or negative even when fiscal deficit is high — interpretation nuance

concepts.name: Monetized Deficit and Ways and Means Advances
key_dimensions: Monetized deficit = increase in net RBI credit to government; direct money creation leading to inflationary pressure
Ways and Means Advances (WMA): temporary overdraft facility by RBI to Centre and States — not permanent financing
1997 agreement: discontinuation of automatic monetization (ad-hoc treasury bills); replaced by market borrowings
UPSC trap: WMA is NOT monetization of deficit; it is a short-term liquidity management tool with interest and repayment

concepts.name: Tax Revenue: Direct vs. Indirect Tax Classification and Devolution
key_dimensions: Direct taxes (income tax, corporation tax) — Centre's exclusive domain; indirect taxes post-GST sharing via IGST mechanism
Divisible pool under Article 270: taxes shared with states per Finance Commission recommendations
UPSC trap: Surcharges and cesses are NOT part of divisible pool — states get no share; political economy implication
Buoyancy vs. elasticity of tax revenue — automatic vs. discretionary response to GDP growth

concepts.name: Non-Tax Revenue: Components and Trends
key_dimensions: Components: interest receipts, dividends from PSUs/RBI, fees, fines, external grants
RBI surplus transfer (Bimal Jalan Committee framework for Economic Capital Framework) as non-tax revenue controversy
Disinvestment proceeds classification: capital receipt (NOT non-tax revenue) — common UPSC trap
Significance of non-tax revenue buoyancy for fiscal consolidation without tax burden increase

concepts.name: Capital Receipts: Borrowings, Disinvestment, and Recovery of Loans
key_dimensions: Three components: (1) borrowings & liabilities, (2) recovery of loans, (3) other receipts including disinvestment
Disinvestment: strategic disinvestment vs. minority stake sale — fiscal and policy implications differ
UPSC trap: Capital receipts are NOT always good — borrowings create future liability; disinvestment is one-time and depletes assets
Monetization of assets (NMP — National Monetisation Pipeline) as a capital receipt strategy distinct from disinvestment

concepts.name: Plan vs. Non-Plan Expenditure Classification (Abolished 2017) and its Replacement
key_dimensions: Pre-2017: Plan expenditure linked to Five-Year Plans; Non-Plan for establishment/interest — criticized for artificial distinction
Replaced from 2017-18 by: Capital vs. Revenue expenditure classification only, on recommendation of C. Rangarajan Committee
Implication: Now focus on whether expenditure creates assets (capital) rather than whether it is under a plan
UPSC trap: Questions still appear on why plan/non-plan was abolished — perverse incentives, operational inflexibility

concepts.name: Voted vs. Charged Expenditure
key_dimensions: Charged expenditure (Article 112(3)): not subject to vote — includes President's salary, judiciary salaries, debt servicing, Speaker's salary
Voted expenditure: requires approval through Demands for Grants in Lok Sabha
UPSC trap: Charged expenditure can be discussed but NOT voted upon in Parliament — subtle but frequently tested distinction
Rajya Sabha's role: can only recommend changes to Demands for Grants, cannot reject — Money Bill asymmetry

concepts.name: Consolidated Fund, Contingency Fund, and Public Account: Tripartite Structure
key_dimensions: Consolidated Fund (Article 266): all revenues, borrowings, and expenditure — Parliamentary approval mandatory
Contingency Fund (Article 267): imprest account of ₹500 crore; executive can draw without Parliament approval for unforeseen expenditure
Public Account (Article 266(2)): provident funds, small savings, securities deposits — NOT government's own money; Parliament's control is procedural not mandatory
UPSC trap: Contingency Fund drawals must be regularized by Parliament later via Supplementary Demands; Public Account transactions are NOT budget expenditure

concepts.name: Types of Budget: Balanced, Surplus, Deficit, and Gender Budget
key_dimensions: Balanced budget: Keynesian criticism (balanced budget multiplier = 1, not expansionary); procyclical in downturns
Surplus budget: appropriate during inflationary periods; India rarely achieves it given developmental needs
Gender Budget: Statement 13 in Union Budget — not a separate budget but a report on gender-disaggregated expenditure
Zero-Based Budgeting vs. Incremental Budgeting — justification from scratch vs. baseline + increment; India's selective adoption

concepts.name: Performance Budget and Outcome Budget: Evolution and Limitations
key_dimensions: Outcome Budget introduced in 2005-06: links financial outlays to physical outcomes/deliverables for each ministry
Performance Budget preceded Outcome Budget — focused on activities rather than outcomes
Limitations: difficulty in quantifying outcomes for social sector; attribution problem; compliance vs. genuine measurement
UPSC relevance: Outcome Budget vs. Expenditure Budget distinction; replaced partially by Output-Outcome Monitoring Framework

concepts.name: Interim Budget vs. Vote on Account vs. Full Budget
key_dimensions: Vote on Account: Parliament's permission to withdraw from Consolidated Fund for a few months pending full budget passage — only covers expenditure
Interim Budget: presented in election year — covers both receipts and expenditure but conventionally avoids major policy announcements
UPSC trap: Interim Budget ≠ Vote on Account — Interim Budget is a complete budget; Vote on Account is a specific parliamentary approval
Constitutional provision: No specific provision for 'Interim Budget' — it is a convention; Vote on Account is under Article 116

concepts.name: Supplementary Demands for Grants and Excess Grants
key_dimensions: Supplementary Demands: when approved allocation is insufficient — presented during the year; must be passed before year-end spending
Excess Grants: post-facto approval by Parliament for spending already incurred beyond approved amount — scrutinized by PAC
Token Demands: when funds are available but parliamentary reappropriation permission needed for new service
UPSC trap: Supplementary grants follow same procedure as regular grants including Money Bill rules; Excess grants require Public Accounts Committee recommendation

concepts.name: FRBM Act 2003: Targets, Escape Clauses, and NK Singh Committee Reforms
key_dimensions: Original targets: eliminate revenue deficit; reduce fiscal deficit to 3% GDP — later amended multiple times
NK Singh Committee (2017): recommended fiscal deficit target of 3% by 2020, debt-to-GDP target of 60% (40% Centre + 20% States) as primary anchor
Escape clause: ±0.5% deviation allowed for national security, calamity, agriculture collapse, structural reforms with revenue implications
UPSC trap: FRBM applies to Centre; States have their own fiscal responsibility laws but must comply with conditions for market borrowings under Article 293(3)

concepts.name: Off-Budget Financing: Concept, Instruments, and Transparency Concerns
key_dimensions: Off-budget borrowings: government directs PSUs/FCI/NABARD to borrow and fund government schemes — not reflected in fiscal deficit
Examples: FCI borrowings from NSSF for food subsidy, NHAI borrowings for highway construction shown as PSU debt
CAG and IMF concerns: understates true fiscal deficit; violates spirit of FRBM transparency norms
UPSC trap: Off-budget liabilities are contingent liabilities of the government even if not in budget — distinction between reported and true fiscal deficit

concepts.name: Subsidies in Budget: Classification, Explicit vs. Implicit, and Rationalization
key_dimensions: Explicit subsidies: food (FCI), fertilizer, petroleum — shown in budget as revenue expenditure; major fiscal burden
Implicit/hidden subsidies: underpricing of government services, tax expenditures (foregone revenue via exemptions) — NOT in budget directly
DBT (Direct Benefit Transfer) as subsidy rationalization tool — reduces leakage but doesn't reduce fiscal cost automatically
UPSC trap: Tax expenditure (revenue foregone statement in budget) is a form of implicit subsidy; presented as Statement 8 in Union Budget documents

concepts.name: Finance Bill vs. Appropriation Bill: Procedural and Constitutional Distinctions
key_dimensions: Finance Bill: gives effect to taxation proposals — classified as Money Bill under Article 110; two types (Finance Bill Category A and B)
Appropriation Bill (Article 114): authorizes withdrawal from Consolidated Fund — cannot be amended to vary amounts or alter destinations
UPSC trap: Finance Bill Category B (e.g., changes affecting Consolidated Fund but not solely tax) may NOT be a Money Bill — requires certification by Speaker
Rajya Sabha cannot amend Appropriation Bill; can only make recommendations on Finance Bill as Money Bill — asymmetric bicameralism in budget
